papers.version_note: Web page of the OpenCyc documentation, last updated 03/28/2002. The text layer is one block with no page breaks; the page is read as 1 page.
papers.what_it_is: Cycorp documentation page describing how the Cyc canonicalizer translates epistemological-level (first-order-logic-like) formulae into heuristic-level clausal constructs.

assertions.value: The authors state that Cyc knowledge is articulated at the epistemological level (EL) as formulae in a notation very similar to first-order logic, and is stored internally at the heuristic level (HL), primarily as formulae in conjunctive-normal form.
quotes: Knowledge is articulated (e.g., by human knowledge engineers, by a front end NL module that is processing text, by a machine learning program, ...) at the epistemological level (EL) as formulae in a notation very similar to first-order logic (FOL).
Knowledge is stored internally at the heuristic level (HL), primarily as formulae in conjunctive-normal form (CNF).
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states the design of the vendor's own system in its introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that separating the articulation representation from the internal representation benefits knowledge engineers, who need only learn a stable representation language, and system designers, who can modify the internal data structures without changing the EL.
quotes: Separating the articulation representation from the internal representation benefits both the knowledge engineers, who need only learn a stable representation language, and the system designers, who are free to modify the internal data structures as needed without changing the EL
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's rationale for its own design; no evidence is given on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that CNF is appropriate for the HL because it maximizes the modularity of the knowledge and supports fast inference algorithms such as clause resolution.
quotes: CNF is appropriate for the HL because it both maximizes the modularity of the knowledge and supports fast inference algorithms (e.g., clause resolution).
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's rationale for its own design; no evidence is given on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state three canonicalization objectives: compression (mapping equivalent EL formulae into a common HL construct), correctness (only equivalent EL formulae are mapped into a common HL construct) and speed.
quotes: (a) compression: mapping equivalent EL formulae into a common HL construct (b) correctness: only equivalent EL formulae are mapped into a common HL construct (c) speed
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the objectives of its own component in the section named for them.

assertions.value: The authors give five equivalent EL formulae about #$sociallyDominates for two dogs that differ by argument order of a symmetric predicate, order of antecedent literals, variable naming, and standard logical transformations such as DeMorgan's Law, and state that adding all five to the Cyc KB results in only one HL construct.
quotes: The second differs from the first only in the order of the arguments to the symmetric predicate #$different .
The fourth differs from the first only by variable naming.
Attempting to add all five formulae to the Cyc KB results in only one HL construct.
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked example stated by the vendor; the page shows no run or output.
assertions.reader_inference: The page asserts the outcome of the example but shows no transcript of the KB.

assertions.value: The authors state that achieving a single HL construct also involves canonicalizing the order of arguments to a commutative relation, in the example #$and.
quotes: Achieving a single HL construct also involves canonicalizing the order of arguments to a commutative relation, in this case #$and .
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states how its own canonicalizer works.

assertions.value: The authors state that users commonly load transcripts of thousands of EL formulae that must each be canonicalized, so canonicalization must be fast, and that the canonicalizer uses a limited set of simplification and transformation rules tuned with hundreds of thousands of examples.
quotes: it is not uncommon for users to load transcripts containing thousands of EL formulae, each of which must be canonicalized.
a limited set of rules for simplifying and transforming formulae that has been tuned with hundreds of thousands of examples
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product; no data are given.

assertions.value: The authors state that efficient translation is directly at odds with detecting and removing duplication, which can involve arbitrary theorem proving, and that the rules are a pragmatic and truth-preserving compromise.
quotes: the goal of efficient translation is directly at odds with the goal of detecting and removing duplication (which can involve arbitrary theorem proving)
These rules reflect a pragmatic compromise between efficiently translating EL formulae into HL constructs and detecting and eliminating duplication, and they are truth-preserving.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states the design trade-off of its own component.

assertions.value: The authors state that not all equivalent formulae simplify to the same expression, so the canonicalizer does not guarantee to map all equivalent EL formulae into a single HL construct, because first-order logic is undecidable; it guarantees soundness and a relatively fast response.
quotes: not all equivalent formulae simplify to the same expression.
the canonicalizer does not (cannot) guarantee to map all equivalent EL formulae into a single HL construct (after all, FOL is undecidable)
it can guarantee soundness (only truly equivalent formulae are mapped into a common HL construct), and it can guarantee a relatively fast response.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states the limit of its own component and gives the undecidability of FOL as the reason.
assertions.reader_inference: The soundness guarantee is asserted, not proved, on this page.

assertions.value: The authors state in an implementation note that canonicalizing the order of arguments to commutative relations obviates commutativity rules, and that this requires every component of the inference engine, including the KB indexing mechanisms, to handle commutativity correctly.
quotes: canonicalizing the order of arguments to commutative relations obviates rules that implement commutativity
This requires that every component of the inference engine (n.b. the KB indexing mechanisms) assume responsibility to correctly handle commutativity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states a design consequence of its own system.

assertions.value: The authors list four canonicalizer components: a critic (tests syntactic and semantic well-formedness), a translation pre-processor (handles exceptions), a translator (maps assertions into CNF and queries into DNF) and a translation post-processor (handles rule macros).
quotes: (a) critic: test for syntactic and semantic well-formedness (b) translation pre-processor: handle exceptions (c) translator: map assertions into CNF, queries into DNF (d) translation post-processor: handle rule macros
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the structure of its own component.

assertions.value: The authors state that the critic checks syntax by parsing with the BNF grammar and checks semantics by enforcing arity constraints and argument constraints, and that ill-formed formulae canonicalize to nil for syntax and to #$True, #$False or nil for semantics.
quotes: The syntactic check simply involves parsing the formulae with the BNF grammar.
Formulae that are not syntactically well-formed canonicalize to nil; formulae that are not semantically well-formed canonicalize to #$True , #$False , or nil.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states the behavior of its own component.

assertions.value: The authors state that CycL relations are declared fixed or variable arity, that fixed arity is declared and constant but may be microtheory specific, that variable arity relations such as #$and and #$different accept zero or more arguments, and that the critic requires each relation to have a declared arity that the argument count satisfies.
quotes: The arity of fixed arity relations is declared and constant (but may be microtheory specific).
Variable arity relations (e.g., #$and , #$different ) accept zero or more arguments.
each relation referenced in a formula has a declared arity (variable or a non-negative integer) and that the number of arguments satisfies the arity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the arity rules of its own language.

assertions.value: The authors state that CycL relations are typed with one or more typing constraints per argument, that function result types can be defined, that all relation typing declarations are microtheory-specific, and that the critic invokes the arg-type module to check them.
quotes: Relations in CycL are typed; one or more typing constraints can be defined for each argument.
All relation typing declarations are microtheory-specific.
The critic invokes the arg-type module to insure that all argument-typing constraints applicable to a formula are satisfied.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the typing rules of its own language.

assertions.value: The authors state in an implementation note that a formula is canonicalized with respect to a designated microtheory, and that canonicalizing the same formula in two different microtheories may produce different results.
assertions.anchor: Implementation note on the critic, p.1
quotes: a formula is canonicalized with respect to a designated microtheory, and canonicalizing the same formula in two different microtheories may produce different results.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states the scope of its own component's behavior.

assertions.value: The authors state that the pre-processor transforms #$ExceptWhen and #$ExceptFor literals into #$abnormal assertions; (#$ExceptWhen <formula-1> <formula-2>) denotes that <formula-2> is default true but is not warranted when <formula-1> holds.
quotes: #$ExceptWhen and #$ExceptFor literals are transformed into #$abnormal assertions.
denotes that <formula-2> is default true, but is not warranted when <formula-1> holds
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the semantics of its own constructs.

assertions.value: The authors state that the pre-processor transforms an #$ExceptWhen formula into (#$implies <formula-1> (#$abnormal <variables> <kb-assertion>)), where <variables> are the EL variables appearing in <formula-2> and <kb-assertion> is the HL construct, already asserted in the Cyc knowledge base, derived from canonicalizing <formula-2>.
quotes: ( #$implies <formula-1> ( #$abnormal <variables> <kb-assertion>))
where <variables> are the EL variables appearing in <formula-2>, and <kb-assertion> is the HL construct, already asserted in the Cyc knowledge base, derived from canonicalizing <formula-2>.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the translation of its own construct.

assertions.value: The authors state that the translator maps assertions into CNF and queries into DNF using a standard algorithm cited to Genesereth and Nilsson, "Logical Foundations of Artificial Intelligence", outlined as six steps.
quotes: assertions are mapped into CNF; queries are mapped into DNF.
see "Logical Foundations of Artificial Intelligence" by Genesereth and Nilsson
the approach is outlined below as six steps
assertions.certainty_reason: The algorithm is attributed to other work; this page only outlines it.

assertions.value: The authors list six translator steps: remove implications, distribute negations, standardize variables, remove existential quantifiers by substituting a unique skolem function, remove universal quantifiers because every variable is unique and universally quantified, and distribute disjunctions and conjunctions into CNF or DNF.
quotes: (1) remove implications:
(3) standardize variables
(4) remove existential quantifiers Substitute a unique skolem function in for every existentially quantified formula.
Since every variable is now unique and universally quantified, all universal quantifiers can be dropped.
(6) distribute disjunctions and conjunctions to put into CNF or DNF
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard algorithm attributed to other work and only outlined here.

assertions.value: The authors give the negation-distribution rules of the second translator step: not-and becomes or-of-nots, not-or becomes and-of-nots, not-forAll becomes thereExists-not, and not-thereExists becomes forAll-not.
quotes: ( #$not ( #$and <formula-1> ...)) -> ( #$or ( #$not <formula-1>) ...)
( #$not ( #$forAll <var> <formula>)) -> ( #$thereExists <var> ( #$not <formula>))
( #$not ( #$thereExists <var> <formula>)) -> ( #$forAll <var> ( #$not <formula>))
assertions.certainty_reason: Standard transformations attributed to other work; the or-to-and-of-nots rule is on the page too.

assertions.value: The authors state that the six steps produce one or more clauses for each well-formed EL formula being canonicalized.
quotes: These six steps produce one or more clauses for each well-formed EL formula being canonicalized.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states the output of its own component.

assertions.value: The authors define a rule macro as a compressed construct, typically a single literal, that denotes or expands into a non-atomic formula, and state that special inference modules typically support each rule macro.
quotes: Each rule macro is a compressed construct (typically a single literal) that denotes or expands into a non-atomic (e.g., disjunctive) formula.
Typically, there are special inference modules that support each rule macro.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the term for its own system.

assertions.value: The authors give #$genls as a rule macro: the formula (#$implies (#$isa ?x #$Poodle) (#$isa ?x #$Dog)) is translated into CNF and then transformed by the post-processor into the literal (#$genls #$Poodle #$Dog), and the inference engine has a special HL module that reasons efficiently with #$genls literals.
quotes: which is then transformed by the post-processor into the literal: ( #$genls #$Poodle #$Dog ).
The inference engine has a special HL module that reasons efficiently with #$genls literals
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked example stated by the vendor; the page shows no run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the post-processor canonicalizes the clause components in three steps: ordering commutative arguments (a decomposing heuristic for non-atomic terms, a simple lexical technique for atomic terms), reifying function terms, and replacing EL variables with HL variables.
quotes: canonicalizing the order of commutative arguments, including a decomposing heuristic technique for canonicalizing the order of non-atomic terms (e.g., literals) and using a simple lexical technique for ordering atomic terms
(b) reifying function terms (c) replacing EL variables with HL variables
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states the procedure of its own component.

assertions.value: The authors state the purposes of the three post-processor steps: ordering commutative arguments avoids adding to the KB two formulae that rephrase each other, reifying function terms supports efficient indexing of assertions in the KB, and replacing EL variables with HL variables supports an efficient unification algorithm.
quotes: The first step is performed in order to avoid redundantly adding to the KB two formulae which simply rephase each other.
The second step is performed in order to support efficient indexing of assertions in the KB
The third step is performed in order to support an effient unification algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's rationale for its own design; no evidence is given.
